sense: of a word or a name: come from, be formed from

terms.gloss: draw, derive (a name, a beginning) from
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation: nōmen, orīginem dūcere ab (or ex) with the ablative
evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.18: ab aliquā rē tōtīus vītae dūcere exōrdium (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. etymology: orīginem dūcere (vel trahere)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to draw, deduce, derive its origin or beginning from”. The first sense is “lead”; ductus has a short u (the voiceless stop before it blocks Lachmann’s law).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with ex or ab and the ablative
evidence: Cic. Phil. 3.16: quī cognōmen ex contumēliā trāxerit (Lewis & Short)
Ov. M. 4.291: nōmen ab illīs (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: be called after, be so named from
terms.grammar: phrase: passive of dīcō, with ab and the ablative, or ab eō quod with a clause
evidence: Varr. LL 5.21: terra dicta ab eō … quod teritur
terms.comment: The grammarians’ way of giving an etymology, true or false: Varro’s is a folk etymology.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, with ab and the ablative
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: in this sense post-Augustan, “for dūcere”. Classically it means to lead off water from a river (Caes. B.G. 7.72), and so to divert (blame, anger) onto someone.

phrases.english: a man who got his surname from an insult

phrases.latin: terra dicta ab eō, ut Aelius scrībit, quod teritur
phrases.english: terra (earth) is so called, as Aelius writes, because it is trodden (a folk etymology)
